title: English oak
summary: The English oak (Quercus robur) is a broad-leaved tree of European woods and parks; a mature one is a living tower of wood that stands for hundreds of years.

layers.basics: An oak is a plant that has turned into a tree: it keeps its stem year after year and adds a new layer of wood to it every growing season. Roots below hold it up and drink; the trunk and branches lift the leaves into the light; the leaves make sugar from air, water and sunlight. Click any part of the tree to meet it. The layer buttons show the wood inside the trunk, the roots under the ground, and the water and sugar that flow through the tree.
layers.deeper: It is a flowering plant (an angiosperm), in the beech family. Each spring it opens new leaves (the date varies from year to year and has moved earlier as springs have warmed), flowers with long yellow catkins, and in autumn drops acorns, each in a shallow cup. It is deciduous: the leaves fall in autumn and the tree rests through winter. Its wood is dense and long-lasting, which is why oak was used for ships and buildings.
layers.expert: As a tree with secondary growth, its trunk widens through the vascular cambium and its crown extends through apical meristems at the shoot tips. The tree supports a very large community of insects, fungi, birds and mammals.

facts: ≈ 20 m (chosen); trunk diameter ≈ 1.0 m at breast height, girth ≈ 3.1 m; crown ≈ 19 m wide
often over 500 years; some believed over 1,000
open_questions: Why do oaks in one area all produce big acorn crops in the same year? Weather cues seem to be involved, but how the trees stay in step is still studied.
did_you_know: Oaks "mast": in some years a tree drops a huge crop of acorns and in others very few. Q. robur crops are irregular: a 27-year record from 12 trees in southern England shows large crops in some years and small ones in others, linked to the weather.

title: Oak trunk
summary: The trunk holds the crown up and carries water and sugar between roots and leaves. At the base it flares out into a root flare that spreads the load.

layers.basics: The trunk is the tree's mast and its pipework. The outside is rough bark. Inside, almost all of it is wood: old, dead wood in the middle that only holds things up, and a thin ring of younger wood near the surface that carries water. Choose "Wood" to see a log cut open.
layers.deeper: Where the trunk meets the ground it widens into root flares. The widening spreads the load of a heavy crown over more ground and joins the trunk to the big roots. Higher up, the trunk forks into limbs. The total cross-section of the limbs above a fork is roughly the same as the cross-section of the trunk below it, as if the tree were built from a bundle of pipes of fixed size.
layers.expert: The "pipe model" (Shinozaki and colleagues, 1964) treats a tree as a bundle of unit pipes, one for each unit of leaf, so a branch's cross-sectional area is about the sum of the areas of the branches it carries. It is an approximation: real trees depart from it with age, species and wind loading. The model oak's limbs are built to this rule.

facts: ≈ 1.0 m across at 1.3 m height (about 3.1 m round), widening to ≈ 1.5 m at the ground
open_questions: How closely real branching follows the pipe model, and why, is still debated.

title: Bark
summary: Bark is everything outside the cambium: a living inner part that carries sugar, and a dead, cracked outer part that protects.

layers.basics: Bark is the tree's skin. It keeps water in, keeps fire, insects and fungi out, and cushions the living layers underneath. On an old oak it is thick, grey-brown and cut by deep vertical furrows. The furrows appear because the trunk keeps getting wider and the dead outer bark cannot stretch, so it cracks.
layers.deeper: Bark has two main layers. The inner bark is the phloem, which is alive and carries sugar. The outer bark is made mostly of dead cells, including cork, that a thin layer of cells called the cork cambium makes year after year. Old outer bark is pushed outwards and eventually flakes off or stays in ridges.
layers.expert: Botanists call the whole outer protective tissue the periderm: the cork cambium (phellogen) makes cork (phellem) on the outside and a thin living layer (phelloderm) on the inside. Cork cells are coated with suberin, a waxy polymer that blocks water. In older trees new cork cambia form deeper in the bark, cutting off outer layers: this is why oak bark builds up as thick ridges. Bark also contains tannins, which defend against pests and which people used to tan leather.

facts: grey-brown, with close vertical grooves in vertical plates
≈ 3 cm (typical for a trunk this size; not measured on a real tree)

title: Cork and cork cambium
summary: Cork is the dead, waterproof outer layer of bark; a thin layer of dividing cells, the cork cambium, makes it.

layers.basics: On the outside of the trunk lies a layer of cells that are dead and filled with air. Their walls are waterproofed with a waxy substance, so the layer works like a raincoat and a draught excluder. A thin sheet of cells just under it keeps dividing to make more.
layers.deeper: The dividing sheet is the cork cambium. It makes cork cells outwards, and a few living cells inwards. As the trunk widens, old cork splits, and the cambium renews it. Cork also lets gas through at small pores called lenticels, so living cells under the bark can still breathe.
layers.expert: Cork cell walls carry suberin, a polyester of fatty acids and aromatic compounds, which makes the layer almost impermeable to water. The cork oak (Quercus suber) makes unusually thick cork, which is harvested for stoppers. English oak makes far less, but the principle is the same.

facts: dead at maturity, walls coated with suberin

title: Inner bark (phloem)
summary: The inner bark is the phloem: living tubes that carry sugar solution from the leaves to wherever the tree is growing or storing food.

layers.basics: Right under the dead outer bark is a thin living layer. Its tubes carry a sweet liquid made in the leaves down the trunk to the roots, and up to buds and acorns. If a ring of bark is cut all the way round the trunk, the tree can no longer send sugar to its roots, and it will eventually die.
layers.deeper: The tubes are made of sieve tube elements, long cells joined end to end, with pores in the end walls. They have no nucleus when mature, so each one is kept alive by a small neighbour called a companion cell. Sugar, mostly sucrose, is pushed along by pressure: the leaves load sugar in, water follows by osmosis, the pressure rises, and the solution flows towards places where sugar is being used.
layers.expert: Phloem transport is described by the pressure-flow (Münch) hypothesis: loading raises sugar concentration and turgor pressure at the source, unloading lowers it at the sink, and bulk flow follows the pressure gradient. Sieve-tube pressures measured so far are of the order of 1 MPa (about 1.1 MPa in the leaves of a climbing vine, Knoblauch et al. 2016); direct measurements in tall trees are scarce. Flow speeds are far lower than in the xylem, and the exact rates vary with tree, season and method. The figure here is drawn thicker than a real trunk's inner bark so it can be seen in the cut log.

facts: both ways, from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, buds, acorns)
positive; ≈ 1 MPa where measured (in a vine)
open_questions: Exactly how the very long sieve tubes of tall trees keep their flow balanced and how far the pressure-flow picture holds in the tallest trees are still being tested.

ext.title: Knoblauch et al. 2016: Testing the Muench hypothesis of long distance phloem transport (eLife)

title: Vascular cambium
summary: The vascular cambium is a thin layer of cells that divide to make new wood inwards and new inner bark outwards. It is how a trunk gets wider.

layers.basics: Between the wood and the bark lies a layer only a few cells thick that never stops dividing while the tree lives. Each year it adds a ring of new wood on its inside and a little new bark on its outside. This is why a trunk grows fatter. The cut log draws this layer much thicker than it is, so you can find it.
layers.deeper: The cambium is a ring of meristem, tissue made of cells that stay able to divide. Daughter cells on the inner side become xylem (wood), those on the outer side become phloem. Because wood is added far faster than bark, the cambium is pushed steadily outwards as the trunk thickens. In temperate trees it works in a yearly rhythm: wide pale cells in spring, narrow dense cells later, which gives each year its ring.
layers.expert: The cambium consists of fusiform initials, which make the long cells of the wood and bark, and ray initials, which make the radial rays. Its activity is regulated by hormones, among them auxin from the growing shoots above, and by temperature and water supply. In the model log, the cambium is about 5 mm thick for visibility; in life the dividing zone is a few cell widths, a fraction of a millimetre.

facts: a few cells (a fraction of a millimetre)
≈ 2π × ring width (e.g. a 3 mm ring adds ≈ 1.9 cm)

title: Sapwood
summary: Sapwood is the younger, outer wood of a trunk. In oak most of the water moves through its outermost ring or two, and the rest of the sapwood stores food.

layers.basics: The pale wood near the outside of a log is the sapwood. Water rises through the outer part of it from the roots to the leaves. The living cells in the sapwood also store sugar and starch that the tree draws on in spring, before new leaves can make food.
layers.deeper: The water travels through dead, hollow tubes (vessels) that are full of water and held under tension, like a rope of water. A vessel that fills with air has failed and no longer carries water. Sapwood and the water-carrying zone are not the same thing. Sapwood is the whole band of wood outside the heartwood, set by colour and by whether the vessels are plugged with tyloses, and in oak it is several rings wide. In the oak that has been measured, most of the flow is in the newest ring (in one veteran English oak the crown's water use needed only the current ring). How many rings the sapwood has depends on where the oak grew: regional studies find averages of about 11 to 15 rings, and single trees range from about 6 to 31. The model log has 13 rings of sapwood, a chosen number inside that range.
layers.expert: Oak is ring-porous: the vessels formed in early spring, the earlywood, are very wide (about 0.5 mm across) and carry most of the water, while the narrow vessels of later wood carry less. A vessel is formed from a stack of cells whose end walls break down and whose living contents die, leaving a pipe. Sapwood ring counts are regional samples and fall from west to east across Europe (means: eastern Baltic 11.5, Pannonian Basin 13.3, Romania 13.1, Czech Republic 14.6, Poland 15; Roibu et al. 2021 summarise them). They are used to estimate the felling date of old timbers, and they rise with tree age. In the sapwood the living cells (parenchyma) store starch.

facts: ≈ 11.5–15 in five European studies; single trees ≈ 6–31 in the Romanian sample
mostly the outermost ring or two

title: Heartwood
summary: Heartwood is the darker, older wood at the centre of a trunk. It no longer carries water, but it holds the tree up and resists rot.

layers.basics: The deep, darker wood in the middle of a log is heartwood. It is not the "living heart" its name suggests. Its job is to hold the tree up. It is darker because the tree stores chemicals in it that make it harder for fungi and insects to feed on it, which is one reason oak timber lasts so long.
layers.deeper: As rings get older, the living cells inside them die in a planned process and the wood fills with protective chemicals. A tree can survive with a rotted heart: the active layers are near the surface. Many old oaks are hollow and still alive for centuries.
layers.expert: Heartwood formation is genetically programmed and happens without injury; the transition zone shows the final death of the living cells and the build-up of extractives such as phenolic compounds. The heartwood of English and sessile oak contains roughly 10 per cent of its dry weight as ellagitannins, water-soluble phenolic compounds that are regarded as the main source of its resistance to rot (Vivas et al. 2004). How much a given tree holds varies widely between trees and is under strong genetic control, so oak heartwood is durable on average, not in every tree. The timber of English oak has a density of about 720 kg per cubic metre.

facts: ≈ 10 % by weight (Q. robur and Q. petraea)
support and decay resistance; no water carrying

title: Annual growth rings
summary: Each ring in a cut trunk is one year of wood. Count the rings and you know the tree's age at that height.

layers.basics: In places with seasons, a tree grows in a yearly rhythm: in spring it builds wide cells for lots of water flow, later it builds smaller, denser ones. On a cut trunk this shows as a pale band and then a darker band, together one ring. Count them from the middle out and you have the number of years. Wide rings mean good years, narrow rings mean poor ones. The cut log has about 150 rings.
layers.deeper: Ring widths are a record of the weather and of the tree's own history, such as a crowded youth or a gap opening in the forest canopy. Scientists match the ring patterns of many trees and old timbers to date wood to the exact year; this is called dendrochronology. Counting at the base tells how old the tree is only if the cut is at ground level, because the tree took some years to reach the height of the cut.
layers.expert: In oak, the earlywood vessels are large and form a clear pore ring, the latewood is dense and darker. Rings are not always one per year: drought or insect defoliation can produce a partial or missing ring, which is why dendrochronologists cross-date against reference series. The model has 150 rings whose widths are random around a plausible trend (wider when young, narrower later); they are not a real tree's record.

facts: Mean ring width in the model
did_you_know: Because wide and narrow years follow the weather, ring patterns from living trees and old beams can be lined up like a barcode to give an exact year for a piece of timber.

title: Pith and wood rays
summary: The pith is the soft core where the shoot began. Rays are thin sheets of living cells that run across the wood from the centre outwards.

layers.basics: At the very middle of a trunk is the pith, a small core of soft tissue that was the centre of the tiny seedling stem. Fine lines run outwards from the middle like the spokes of a wheel. These are rays, sheets of living cells that carry food sideways across the rings and store it.
layers.deeper: Rays are the one part of the wood that runs radially (outwards) and not up and down. They let sugar from the inner bark reach the living cells deep in the sapwood. In oak some rays are broad enough to see without a lens, and they make the silvery "fleck" pattern in quarter-sawn oak boards.
layers.expert: Wood rays are made by the ray initials of the cambium. Oak has two kinds: many narrow rays one cell wide, and fewer wide rays that are about 10 to 30 cells wide (the standard wood-anatomy description of the genus). In the model log the rays are drawn as pale radial streaks on the cut faces; their number, length and spacing are illustrative.

facts: ≈ 1.2 cm across (drawn larger than real, for visibility)

ext.title: Wood anatomy of Quercus (IAWA description, Richter and Dallwitz)

title: Oak branches
summary: Branches carry leaves out into the light. An oak in the open spreads wide, with a few huge limbs low down.

layers.basics: An oak grown in the open has thick, crooked limbs that reach out sideways and form a wide dome, because there is light on all sides. An oak in a dense wood grows tall and straight with a narrow crown as it competes upward. Each branch splits again and again until the twigs that carry leaves.
layers.deeper: Each branch grows at its tip, and new side branches grow from buds. A branch's thickness matches the amount of branching it carries, so thick limbs near the trunk thin step by step to twigs. The model's branches are grown by a computer rule in which each tip grows toward free space with light, then thickened by the pipe rule.
layers.expert: The shape of the crown comes from apical dominance, shedding of shaded lower branches, and repeated damage and regrowth that give the crooked, massive look of old oaks. The branching in this model is generated by space colonisation, an algorithm that grows a skeleton toward points scattered in a crown-shaped volume, not from measurements of one real tree.

facts: wide, unevenly domed, with massive lower branches

title: Twigs and buds
summary: Twigs are this year's thin shoots. Each ends in a cluster of buds that hold next year's growth folded up inside.

layers.basics: A twig is a young branch. At its tip sits a bud: a tiny package of unopened leaves wrapped in scales. In winter the tree is bare and the buds wait. In spring they swell and open. Oaks have buds grouped in a cluster at the end of each twig.
layers.deeper: Each bud holds a miniature shoot with leaves already formed, which is why a tree can open its leaves in days. Buds at the tip carry on the main shoot; buds along the side make branches. Scars left where bud scales fell away mark the year's boundary on the twig, so you can read the age of a twig.
layers.expert: Buds contain apical meristems. Dormancy is set by day length and temperature: a tree needs enough cold in winter and then warmth in spring before it breaks bud, which is why a warming climate changes the date of leaf-out. In a UK study of eleven tree species, bud burst in nine of them followed the average March temperature, coming earlier after a warmer March (Met Office, 2017). The leaves, buds and twigs in the model are drawn to typical sizes and are placed by a rule, not copied from a real branch.

facts: varies with the year and the place; earlier after a warm March

ext.title: Met Office 2017: Earlier budburst linked to warmer springs

title: Oak leaf
summary: The leaf is a thin, flat solar panel and chemical factory: it takes in carbon dioxide and light and makes sugar. Click Look inside to see its layers.

layers.basics: An oak leaf is shaped like a long paddle with rounded lobes along each side. It is about 10 cm long and held on a very short stalk. Its flat shape catches light. Its green colour comes from chlorophyll, the molecule that captures sunlight. Inside, the leaf is only a fraction of a millimetre thick. Choose "Look inside the leaf" to go there.
layers.deeper: The leaf takes in carbon dioxide through tiny pores, mostly on its underside, and uses light energy to join the carbon to water, making sugar and releasing oxygen. A network of veins brings water in and carries sugar out. The lobes of the English oak's leaf are rounded and cut in no deeper than halfway to the midrib. It drops its leaves in autumn.
layers.expert: English oak leaves are about 10–12 cm long and 7–8 cm wide, with 3–6 rounded lobes, and a leaf stalk (petiole) of only 2–3 mm. The leaf is hypostomatous, meaning the stomata are on the underside; one study of 17 genotypes counted 530–791 per square millimetre. The model has about 18,700 leaves; that count is illustrative, not a count of a real tree.

facts: 3–6, rounded, cut no deeper than halfway

ext.title: Stomata and leaf trichome characteristics in Quercus robur genotypes (record)

title: Leaf cuticle and epidermis
summary: The outer skin of a leaf: a waxy waterproof coat and a single layer of flat cells beneath it.

layers.basics: A leaf must let light and air in but keep water from escaping. The outer cells form a skin, and on top of it is a thin waxy layer, the cuticle. Together they are a raincoat for the leaf. The cuticle is thicker on the top (sun) side than the underside.
layers.deeper: The epidermis is one layer of tightly joined cells without chloroplasts, except for the pairs of guard cells. Being clear and flat, they let light through to the cells below. The cuticle is made of cutin and wax and is thinner on the lower epidermis than on the upper in most leaves.
layers.expert: Epidermal cells secrete the cuticle. Leaves in dry climates tend to have a thicker cuticle. The scene's dimensions are illustrative: the layers are drawn at relative sizes typical of a broadleaf leaf, not measured on oak.

facts: cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll, lower epidermis, cuticle

title: Palisade mesophyll
summary: Tall, tightly packed cells just under the top surface, filled with chloroplasts: the main light-catching layer.

layers.basics: Right below the top skin stand rows of tall, narrow cells, like fence posts, packed shoulder to shoulder. They face the sun and are crammed with chloroplasts, the green parts that capture light. This is where most of the leaf's sugar-making happens.
layers.deeper: Their column shape lets light pass down the long cells while the chloroplasts line the walls. Most flowering plants have one to two layers of palisade cells; leaves in full sun can have more. In the scene each palisade cell holds only a few chloroplasts to keep the picture readable.
layers.expert: Chloroplast number varies from one in some algae to many dozens (up to about 100 in Arabidopsis and wheat) per mesophyll cell. Light is absorbed as it passes down the leaf so the upper layers do most of the photosynthesis and the lower layers use light scattered by the cell walls. The proportions drawn are typical, not measured on oak.

facts: 1–2 cells thick in most flowering plants
many dozens, up to ≈ 100 in some species

title: Spongy mesophyll
summary: Loosely packed cells with air gaps between them, below the palisade layer, where gases move through the leaf.

layers.basics: Below the fence-post cells lies a looser layer of rounder cells with air gaps between them. Carbon dioxide comes in through the pores below and spreads through these gaps to reach every cell, and oxygen and water vapour leave the same way. These cells also have chloroplasts.
layers.deeper: The gaps form a connected network of air spaces so gases can reach cells deep in the leaf. Gases dissolve in the thin film of water on the cell walls, then enter the cell. Water leaving the leaf as vapour comes out through the same spaces.
layers.expert: The air spaces make up a large share of the leaf's internal volume; the total area of the cell walls facing the air is many times the area of the leaf itself, which is what makes gas uptake fast enough. The exact internal-space fraction varies with the species and the light the leaf grew in.

facts: gas exchange between pores and cells
present, fewer than in palisade cells

title: Stoma and guard cells
summary: A stoma is a pore in the leaf skin between two bean-shaped guard cells that open and close it.

layers.basics: Stomata (one is a stoma) are the leaf's breathing holes. Two curved cells, the guard cells, sit side by side. When they swell with water they bend apart and open a gap. When they lose water they straighten and shut it. Open, the leaf takes in carbon dioxide but loses water vapour. Closed, it saves water but cannot make sugar.
layers.deeper: Guard cells respond to light, to the leaf's water supply and to the carbon dioxide level inside. In the daytime, with enough water, they open. In a drought, a plant hormone tells them to close. Guard cells are the only cells of the epidermis with chloroplasts. English oak has its stomata on the underside, hundreds per square millimetre.
layers.expert: Opening works by osmosis: potassium and other ions flow into the guard cells, water follows, and the cells swell. Their walls are stiffer on the side facing the pore, so swelling bends the cell apart. Stomatal density across species ranges widely (1,000 to 100,000 per cm² in general; 530–791 per mm² measured across 17 pedunculate oak genotypes).

facts: the only epidermal cells with chloroplasts

ext.title: Stomata and leaf trichome characteristics in Quercus robur genotypes (record)

title: Leaf vein
summary: A vein is a small bundle of pipes in the leaf: water arrives in the xylem, sugar leaves in the phloem.

layers.basics: Veins are the leaf's plumbing. Each one holds two kinds of tubes side by side. The ones on the top side bring in water from the twig. The ones on the underside carry the sugar made in the leaf out to the rest of the tree. Veins branch into a fine net so that no cell is far from one.
layers.deeper: The xylem sits on the upper side of the bundle and the phloem on the lower side. A sheath of cells around the bundle controls what passes between the veins and the leaf cells. Water leaving the vein spreads through the cell walls to the cells that need it.
layers.expert: The xylem conduits are dead, hollow tubes filled with water, so water in them flows by the pull of evaporation at the leaf, not by pushing. Phloem sieve tubes are living but lack a nucleus and are served by companion cells. For an ideal smooth tube the flow rises with the fourth power of its diameter (the Hagen-Poiseuille law), so a few wide tubes carry a great deal; real vessels carry somewhat less than this ideal.

facts: rises with diameter to the 4th power

title: Acorn and oak reproduction
summary: An acorn is an oak's fruit: a single nut holding one seed, sitting in a scaly cup. Each one could grow into a new tree.

layers.basics: In spring an oak makes two kinds of flowers on the same tree. Long yellow catkins hang down and shed pollen on the wind. Tiny female flowers further up the twig receive it. By autumn the fertilised flowers have become acorns, each in a cup. Most acorns are eaten by animals, and a few are buried and forgotten, and sprout.
layers.deeper: The wind-blown pollen carries the male sex cells; the female flower holds the egg cell. After fertilisation the seed forms inside the nut, with a store of food that feeds the seedling. Jays and squirrels bury acorns and help the oak spread. English oak acorns are 1.5–4 cm long and hang on a stalk of 4–8 cm, two or three together. Some years the tree makes many acorns, and some years few.
layers.expert: The oak is monoecious and wind-pollinated. Mast seeding (large synchronised crops) swamps seed predators so that some seeds survive. Large crops come at irregular intervals: in a 27-year record of acorn yield from 12 trees in southern England, mast years were linked to the weather (Hanley, Cook and Fenner 2019). Acorn length varies; the model uses a nut about 2.5 cm long.

facts: 105, hung on the sprigs (a model choice)

ext.title: Hanley, Cook and Fenner 2019: Climate variation, reproductive frequency and acorn yield in English oaks (J. Plant Ecology)

did_you_know: A single acorn contains an entire oak: a small root, shoot and a store of food, packaged in a nut.

title: Oak roots
summary: Roots anchor the tree and take up water and minerals from the soil. Most of the root system is far thinner than you can see.

layers.basics: Below ground, an oak has roots that reach as far across as the crown does above ground, or further. Big roots near the trunk hold the tree and carry water; smaller ones branch off them and, at the ends, are very fine roots that do the drinking. Choose "Roots" to see through the ground.
layers.deeper: The very fine roots, finer than a pencil lead, take up almost all the water and minerals. They are short-lived and are replaced all the time. The big roots store sugar and hold the tree upright against the wind. The root system draws its shape from the soil: roots go where the water and nutrients are.
layers.expert: Roots take up water by osmosis, with the greatest absorption near the tips where root hairs form. Many trees put most of their roots into the upper layers of soil, where oxygen, water and nutrients are, but the pattern varies with soil and species. The root system in the model is a schematic made by a growth rule, not a map of a real tree's roots, and the fine roots are far fewer than in real life.

facts: water and dissolved minerals, mostly at fine root tips
schematic; real oak root systems differ with soil
open_questions: How the total mass of fine roots in a forest changes through the seasons and with a warming climate is hard to measure and still being studied.

title: Root tip and root hairs
summary: Root hairs are tiny tubes growing from the cells of a young root that multiply its surface for taking up water.

layers.basics: Just behind the tip of a young root, some skin cells grow a thin, hair-like tube out into the soil. Each is a single cell. A root covered in hairs touches far more soil than a bare root could, so it can reach more water in the soil between grains.
layers.deeper: The root tip is protected by a cap and has a growing zone behind it where cells divide and then lengthen. Root hairs form a little further back in the zone where cells mature. They live only days to weeks. Oak is one of the trees whose fine root tips are wrapped in a fungal sleeve (see the mycorrhiza card), and the fungus does part of this job.
layers.expert: Root hairs are outgrowths of epidermal cells. They greatly increase the root surface area and so the uptake of water and mineral ions, particularly phosphate that moves slowly in soil. Ectomycorrhizal root tips are covered with fungus and produce few or no root hairs, so the root-hair scene (reached by zooming into root tissue) shows the general case of a bare fine root, not the usual oak tip; the close-up from the fine roots in the oak and the soil shows a fungus-wrapped tip instead.

facts: one cell, lives days to weeks
larger surface for water and mineral uptake

title: Mycorrhiza: the oak's fungal partners
summary: Oak roots partner with underground fungi: the tree supplies sugar, and the fungal threads gather water and minerals from the soil.

layers.basics: Oak roots are wrapped in a sheath of fungus. The fungus sends fine white threads out into the soil, far beyond the root, where they collect water and minerals. In return the tree gives the fungus sugar made in its leaves. How much each side gains depends on the soil and the conditions.
layers.deeper: This kind of partnership is called ectomycorrhiza. The fungus makes a mantle around the root tip and grows between the root cells without entering them. The oak family and the pine family are among the plants that do this. A single tree usually hosts more than one fungal species at once. Some of them make the mushrooms you find under oaks in autumn.
layers.expert: The fungus supplies water and minerals such as phosphorus and nitrogen and receives photosynthetic carbon. Only about 2% of plant species form ectomycorrhiza (72% form the arbuscular kind; Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018), though many of them are dominant trees. The wider claim that trees are joined into forest-wide "common mycorrhizal networks" that share carbon and warning signals is contested. Karst, Jones and Hoeksema (2023) reviewed the evidence: the claims that such networks are widespread in forests and that they pass resources to improve seedling growth are insufficiently supported, because field results vary too widely or have other explanations; the claim that mature trees preferentially send resources and defence signals to their offspring through them has no peer-reviewed evidence; and they found that unsupported claims in the citing literature have doubled in 25 years. Researchers who defend carbon transfer between trees have replied, so this is an active dispute.

facts: ectomycorrhiza (fungus around and between root cells)
sugar from the tree; water and minerals from the fungus
open_questions: Do trees share meaningful amounts of carbon and chemical signals through fungal networks that join them in real forests? Karst and colleagues (2023) judge the evidence too sparse and unsettled; others disagree, and the question is open.

ext.title: Brundrett and Tedersoo 2018: Evolutionary history of mycorrhizal symbioses and global host plant diversity (New Phytologist)

title: Cellulose and lignin: what wood is made of
summary: Wood is mainly cellulose fibres glued and stiffened by lignin.

layers.basics: The strength of wood comes from two materials. Cellulose is long chains of sugar molecules bundled into tough fibres. Lignin is a hard, brown, glue-like substance that fills the spaces between the fibres and makes the wall rigid and waterproof. It is rather like steel rods set in concrete.
layers.deeper: Every plant cell wall has cellulose. Wood cells, after they finish growing, build a thick second wall with lignin and then usually die, leaving a hard hollow shell. Lignin makes vessels strong enough to hold water under strong pull without collapsing.
layers.expert: Cellulose is a polymer of β-glucose units, shown in the molecule viewer as the three-sugar fragment cellotriose; microfibrils of many chains are held by hydrogen bonds. Lignin is a cross-linked polymer built from phenolic alcohols and is one of the most abundant organic polymers on Earth after cellulose.

facts: cross-linked phenolic polymer that stiffens cell walls

title: How an oak lifts water 20 metres
summary: Water climbs through the oak because evaporation from the leaves pulls on a continuous chain of water molecules; the tree uses no pump.

layers.basics: Water evaporates from the leaves. Because water molecules stick to each other, the evaporation pulls the whole column of water in the wood upwards, like sucking a drink through a straw. The tree does not push the water from below; it is pulled from above, using the energy of sunlight that drives the evaporation.
layers.deeper: The pulling puts the water in the wood under tension, a negative pressure. This is possible because the narrow tubes are lined with wall that water sticks to and water molecules cohere strongly. Lifting a column 20 m against gravity alone needs a pressure difference of about 0.2 MPa; the real pull is bigger, because the water also has to be forced through the narrow tubes.
layers.expert: The weight of a water column is about 9.8 kPa per metre of height (density times gravitational acceleration), so 20 m needs about 0.2 MPa: this is a calculation, not a measurement of an oak. Real xylem tensions in trees are several times larger because of friction. A conference abstract on mature English oaks at a UK site reports a daily water use of about 2.4 litres per millimetre of trunk radius across trees of 274 to 465 mm radius, with peak sap flux around 0.04 litres per second. In oak the cohesion-tension picture requires the water to stay liquid under tension in vessels that are full of water; a vessel that fills with air is out of action (Venturas et al. 2017).

facts: Daily water use, mature oaks (UK abstract)
≈ 2.4 L per mm of trunk radius (radius 274–465 mm)
open_questions: The tallest trees push the cohesion–tension limit; how they avoid or repair air bubbles in their water columns is still being researched.

ext.title: Water use of mature oaks at BIFoR FACE (EGU23-6064, abstract)

title: How an oak grows wider and taller
summary: A tree grows taller from the tips of its shoots and wider from a thin layer under the bark.

layers.basics: An oak gets taller and longer-limbed because the tips of its shoots and roots keep growing. It gets wider because the layer just under the bark, the cambium, keeps adding a new ring of wood each year. Taller growth happens in spring and early summer; wider growth continues until autumn.
layers.deeper: The two kinds of growth use two different groups of dividing cells. At the tips are apical meristems, which add length. Along the trunk, branches and roots is the vascular cambium, which adds width. Wood laid down in earlier years does not move: a nail hammered into the trunk stays at the same height as the tree grows taller.
layers.expert: Primary growth (from apical meristems) makes the new shoots and roots; secondary growth (from the vascular and cork cambia) thickens them. The share of the year's carbon spent on wood, leaves, roots and acorns is a balance the tree adjusts with the season and with stress, and is not the same every year.

facts: apical meristems at shoot and root tips
vascular cambium, one ring a year

title: What lives on an oak
summary: A single oak is a whole community: insects, fungi, lichens, birds and mammals live in or on it.

layers.basics: An old oak is like a small town. Caterpillars and beetles eat the leaves and wood. Birds nest in its holes and eat the insects. Jays and squirrels bury its acorns. Lichens and mosses grow on the bark. Fungi live in its roots and rot its dead heartwood, making cavities for bats and owls.
layers.deeper: A database of oak-associated life in the UK lists about 2,300 species of birds, mosses, fungi, invertebrates, lichens and mammals that use oak, with each one classed from oak-only to found on many trees. Among the insects are gall-formers, which trick the leaf into growing a ball around their egg. Dead and dying oak wood is also a habitat in its own right.
layers.expert: Counts of "associated species" depend on how association is defined and on how well each group has been surveyed, and Britain's figures cannot be transferred to other parts of Europe without caution. The 2019 OakEcol database gave about 2,300 associated species in the UK.

ext.title: OakEcol: a database of oak-associated biodiversity within the UK (Data in Brief 2019)

title: How long oaks live
summary: English oaks often live over 500 years, and a few may live much longer.

layers.basics: An oak that has been left to grow can see many human generations. Many English oaks are over 500 years old. A few ancient trees are believed to be more than 1,000 years old. They get there partly by letting parts of themselves die: old oaks often lose branches and heartwood and keep growing from what is left.
layers.deeper: The age of very old oaks is usually an estimate, because their centres are hollow and their rings cannot be counted. Age is then estimated from the trunk's girth and from the size of younger trees with known ages, which carries large uncertainty.
layers.expert: Two named trees, the Stelmužė Oak and the Granit Oak, are estimated at more than 1,500 years old. These are estimates, not countable rings. Heart rot hollows the trunk, which removes the oldest rings, so the true age of a hollow oak is not directly knowable.

open_questions: How old is the oldest oak? For a hollow tree the answer is an estimate, and different methods disagree.
